concept_html:
Any clustering algorithm returns clusters, even on random data. Before a cluster becomes a "theme" in a report, check three things.

1. Separation. The silhouette score compares each point's distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other cluster. It runs from -1 to 1, higher is better. scikit-learn 1.8: silhouette_score(X, labels). Compute it without noise points. The function treats -1 as a cluster like any other. In this course's build, four blobs with HDBSCAN noise scored 0.70 with noise removed and 0.555 with noise counted as a cluster.

2. Stability. Rerun the whole pipeline on resampled data, or with different seeds, and compare the labels on the points both runs share. The adjusted Rand index (adjusted_rand_score) is 1 for identical groupings, around 0 for chance, and ignores label names: [0, 0, 1, 1] against [1, 1, 0, 0] scores 1.0. Themes that appear in only some runs are artefacts of the settings.

3. Meaning. Read 10 to 20 answers per cluster. Have two people name the clusters independently, then compare. A cluster nobody can name consistently is not a theme yet.

Report with each theme:

  • its size and share, with noise reported separately,
  • the silhouette and stability figures for the clustering as a whole,
  • three verbatim example answers, chosen at random, not the most typical ones.

No single number proves clusters are real. Together, separation, stability and human reading make a defensible case. Keep the validation results in the run record with the settings (lesson B6-L2).

lines: import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, silhouette_score
def silhouette_without_noise(X: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> float | None:
"""Silhouette over clustered points only. None if fewer than two clusters remain."""
keep = labels != -1
kept = labels[keep]
n_clusters = len(np.unique(kept))
if n_clusters < 2 or n_clusters >= len(kept):
return None
return float(silhouette_score(X[keep], kept))
def stability(labels_a: np.ndarray, labels_b: np.ndarray) -> float:
"""Agreement of two labelings of the same points, ignoring label names."""
return float(adjusted_rand_score(labels_a, labels_b))

exercises.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score


def silhouette_without_noise(X: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> float | None:
    """Silhouette over clustered points only.

    Args:
        X: Feature matrix.
        labels: Cluster labels, -1 for noise.

    Returns:
        The silhouette score, or None when it is undefined.
    """
    keep = labels != -1
    kept = labels[keep]
    n_clusters = len(np.unique(kept))
    if n_clusters < 2 or n_clusters >= len(kept):
        return None
    return float(silhouette_score(X[keep], kept))

title: Validate clusters before you name them
why_html: An insight team presented seven "customer mindsets" from a clustering of attitude statements. A year later a new team reran the same method on a fresh sample. Three of the seven mindsets reappeared. The other four had been unstable from the start: a stability check, rerunning on bootstrap samples, would have shown them splitting and merging from run to run. Two product launches had been planned around mindsets that did not exist.
